name: Bermuda Rose
description: Gin with apricot brandy and grenadine, sharpened with lemon. Pink, stone-fruited and entirely of its decade.
funFact: Apricot brandy in interwar bar books means an apricot liqueur, not a distilled eau-de-vie — buying the wrong bottle turns half the Savoy unmakeable.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Blackthorn
description: Irish whiskey, dry vermouth and absinthe with Angostura. Softer than a Sazerac and sharper than a Manhattan.
funFact: A second, unrelated Blackthorn made with sloe gin exists in the same books — the name attaches to the blackthorn shrub, which gives both sloes and shillelaghs.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.

Express the garnish over the surface and serve.

name: Charlie Chaplin
description: Equal parts sloe gin, apricot brandy and lime. Invented at the Waldorf while Chaplin was the most famous man alive.
funFact: The Waldorf-Astoria named it during Chaplin's peak, when he was arguably the most recognisable person on earth — an equal-parts drink for a man who needed no introduction.

name: Claridge

funFact: Named for the Hôtel Claridge on the Champs-Élysées rather than the London hotel, which spells its name with an apostrophe and served different drinks entirely.

name: Cornell
description: Gin, maraschino and egg white shaken to a pale foam — the quietest of the American college cocktails.
funFact: Cornell, Yale, Princeton and Harvard all acquired cocktails in the 1900s; the drinks have nothing in common beyond the hotel bars that named them.

name: Deep Sea
description: Gin and dry vermouth with absinthe and orange bitters. A Martini pulled toward anise and further out to sea.
funFact: Absinthe in dashes rather than measures is the interwar house style: enough to perfume a drink, never enough to lead it.

name: Delmonico
description: Gin, brandy and both vermouths with orange bitters — named for the restaurant that invented American fine dining.
funFact: Delmonico's opened in 1837 and is credited with the first à la carte menu in America, along with eggs Benedict and lobster Newberg.

name: Dubonnet Cocktail
description: Gin and Dubonnet, two to one, with a lemon twist. The Queen's drink, reportedly taken daily before lunch.
funFact: Queen Elizabeth II's preference for gin and Dubonnet was well enough known that a 1950s note in her own hand requesting one was later sold at auction.

name: Emerald
description: A Manhattan made with Irish whiskey. Lighter, grassier and unaccountably rare on menus.
funFact: Irish whiskey outsold Scotch worldwide before Prohibition and the Irish War of Independence between them destroyed its export trade; the category took eighty years to recover.

description: Gin, triple sec and lemon with a dash of Angostura — a White Lady with bitters and no egg.
funFact: The gin sour with orange liqueur is the single most repeated shape in the Savoy, appearing under at least a dozen names with only the garnish or a dash separating them.

funFact: Named for the ghost ship of North Sea legend, a story Dutch and English sailors traded for centuries before Wagner set it to music.

funFact: It won a London hotel competition in 1930, and the grenadine sunrise it is named for predates the Tequila Sunrise by four decades.

name: Green Dragon
description: Gin, kümmel, green crème de menthe and lemon with peach bitters. Caraway and mint, which is stranger than it sounds.
funFact: Kümmel is a caraway and fennel liqueur that survives in Britain almost entirely because golf clubs kept ordering it as a cure for the shakes on the first tee.

funFact: It predates the American tiki craze by twenty years; the interwar fashion for Polynesian names ran well ahead of any Polynesian drinks.

name: Jockey Club
description: Gin, crème de noyaux, lemon and two bitters. Almond and juniper in a short, dry glass.
funFact: Almond notes in cocktails come from three unrelated places — noyaux from stone fruit kernels, orgeat from real almonds, and amaretto from either.

funFact: The Savoy is full of imperative titles — Leave It To Me, Between the Sheets, Hanky Panky — which reads as a house voice rather than coincidence.

funFact: Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop on Bourbon Street claims to be among the oldest structures used as a bar in the United States, built in the 1720s and still lit largely by candle.

name: Palm Beach

funFact: Grapefruit was still a novelty when this was written — Florida's groves only reached the northern market once refrigerated rail cars made the trip viable.

funFact: Tinned pineapple juice reached British bars in the 1920s and appears all over the Savoy — one of the first industrially processed ingredients the cocktail canon absorbed.

name: Perfect Lady
description: Gin, peach brandy, lemon and egg white — a competition winner from 1936 and a White Lady with stone fruit.
funFact: It won the 1936 British Empire Cocktail Competition, an annual contest that shaped London drinking more than any single bar did.

name: Prince's Smile
description: Gin, calvados and apricot with lemon. Apple and stone fruit over juniper, and drier than the fruit list suggests.
funFact: Calvados appears throughout the interwar books because Normandy apple brandy was cheap and plentiful in London; it went scarce after the war and the drinks went with it.

name: Princeton
description: Gin and port, layered rather than mixed, with orange bitters. The port sits underneath and stays there.
funFact: The original instruction is to pour the port carefully so it settles below the gin — a layered Martini, and one of very few stirred drinks meant to be served unmixed.

steps: Stir the gin and orange bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Pour the port slowly down the side so it settles beneath the gin.
Serve without stirring; the layers are the point.

name: Racquet Club
description: Gin and dry vermouth with orange bitters — a club Martini, and the bitters are not optional.
funFact: Orange bitters were standard in Martinis until the 1940s and then vanished for fifty years; nearly every pre-war Martini variant assumes them.

description: Gin, both vermouths and a dash of Bénédictine. Smooth, herbal and named to sell itself.
funFact: Naming a cocktail after a luxury marque was standard interwar practice — the Rolls-Royce, the Hispano-Suiza and the Bentley all have drinks.

name: Royal Smile
description: Gin, calvados, grenadine and lemon. Pink, appley and one of the better Savoy fruit sours.
funFact: Real grenadine is pomegranate, not cherry — the artificially flavoured red syrup that replaced it in the 1950s is responsible for a generation dismissing these drinks.

funFact: Kümmel has been made in the Low Countries since the sixteenth century, and the same caraway-and-fennel formula turns up in Scandinavian aquavit under a different name.

funFact: There are at least three unrelated Sunshine Cocktails in print between 1900 and 1940, which is roughly the base rate for optimistic cocktail names.

funFact: The tango reached London around 1913 and caused enough moral panic that some hotels banned it — the cocktail arrived with the dance.

funFact: Nobody has established what Ulanda refers to — it is one of a handful of Savoy names with no traceable origin at all.

funFact: The British Empire Exhibition at Wembley drew 27 million visitors across 1924 and 1925, and left behind the stadium and a handful of cocktails.

funFact: Egg white in a sour is doing structural work rather than adding flavour — it emulsifies the citrus oils and holds the aromatics at the surface.

description: Scotch, dry vermouth, absinthe and grenadine with orange bitters. Named for a First World War shell.
funFact: A whizz-bang was a German field shell whose shriek arrived barely before the explosion; soldiers' slang moved straight onto interwar drinks lists.

funFact: The daisy family — spirit, citrus liqueur and lemon over ice — is one of the oldest cocktail templates, and the Margarita is a tequila daisy by another name.
